questions.stem: A great circle is a circle on the Earth's surface:
options: that is parallel to the equator at any latitude
whose radius is half the radius of the Earth
whose centre is the centre of the Earth
that passes through the North and South Poles only
questions.explanation: A great circle is the largest circle that can be drawn on a sphere, and its centre is the Earth's centre. The equator is a great circle, but other parallels of latitude are smaller circles.

questions.stem: Which of these is a great circle?
questions.explanation: The equator is the only parallel of latitude whose centre is the centre of the Earth. Every other parallel, including the Tropic of Capricorn, is a smaller circle.

questions.stem: The latitude of a place is its angle:
options: north or south of the equator
east or west of the prime meridian
north or south of the prime meridian
east or west of the equator
questions.explanation: Latitude measures position north or south of the equator, from 0° at the equator to 90° at each pole. Position east or west of the prime meridian is longitude.

questions.stem: Longitude is measured east or west of:
questions.explanation: Longitude is the angle east or west of the prime meridian (0°), which passes through Greenwich in London. It runs from 0° to 180°E or 180°W.

questions.stem: The latitude of the South Pole is:
questions.explanation: Latitude runs from 0° at the equator to 90° at each pole, so the South Pole is at 90°S. 180° is the largest value of longitude, not latitude.

questions.stem: A place has coordinates 25.3°S, 131.0°E. It lies in:
questions.explanation: S means south of the equator, so the place is in the Southern Hemisphere, and E means east of the prime meridian, so it is in the Eastern Hemisphere. All of Australia lies in these two hemispheres.

questions.stem: A latitude of 27°28′S written in decimal degrees, correct to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: There are 60 minutes in a degree, so 28′ = 28 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.47°, giving 27.47°S. Writing 27.28° treats the minutes as hundredths of a degree.

questions.stem: A longitude of 153.03°E written in degrees and minutes is closest to:
questions.explanation: Multiply the decimal part by 60: 0.03 × 60 = 1.8′, which is about 2′, giving 153°2′E. Reading 0.03 as 3 minutes skips the conversion.

questions.stem: Two places on the same meridian lie at 20°N and 35°S. Their angular distance is:
questions.explanation: The places are on opposite sides of the equator, so their latitudes are added: 20° + 35° = 55°. Subtracting, which gives 15°, is only correct when both are on the same side of the equator.

questions.stem: The meridian 40°E and one other meridian together make up a complete great circle. The other meridian is:
questions.explanation: A meridian runs from pole to pole, and it joins the meridian on the opposite side of the Earth to form a great circle. That meridian is 180° away: 180° − 40° = 140° on the other side of the prime meridian, so 140°W. 40°W is a mirror image, only 80° away.

questions.stem: A town lies 600 km due north of the equator, on the prime meridian. Its position, using D = 111.2 × angular distance, is closest to:
questions.explanation: The angular distance is 600 ÷ 111.2 ≈ 5.4°, measured north of the equator, so the latitude is 5.4°N. Being on the prime meridian makes the longitude 0°, and latitude is always stated first.

questions.stem: On the Earth, a distance of 1° of angular distance along a meridian (great circle) is approximately:
questions.explanation: The formula D = 111.2 × angular distance gives about 111.2 km for each degree along a great circle such as a meridian. 15 relates to time (15° per hour), not distance.

questions.stem: Two towns on the same meridian are at 12°S and 40°S. The distance between them is closest to:
questions.explanation: Both are south of the equator, so the angular distance is 40° − 12° = 28°, and D = 111.2 × 28 = 3113.6 km. Adding the latitudes gives 52° and 5782 km, which would be correct only if the towns were on opposite sides of the equator.

questions.stem: Two places on the same meridian lie at 20°N and 35°S. The distance between them is closest to:
questions.explanation: The angular distance is 20° + 35° = 55°, so D = 111.2 × 55 = 6116 km. Using 35° − 20° = 15° gives 1668 km, the wrong angular distance for places on opposite sides of the equator.

questions.stem: Two places on the same meridian are 1668 km apart. Their angular distance is:
questions.explanation: Rearranging D = 111.2 × angular distance gives 1668 ÷ 111.2 = 15°. This is the reverse of the distance calculation.

questions.stem: A ship at 15°S sails due north along its meridian for 2224 km. Its new latitude is:
questions.explanation: The angular distance travelled is 2224 ÷ 111.2 = 20°. Moving 20° north from 15°S takes the ship 15° to the equator and 5° beyond, so it reaches 5°N. 35°S would be the result of sailing south instead.

questions.stem: For two places on the same parallel of latitude θ, the distance between them along the parallel is calculated with:
questions.explanation: A parallel at latitude θ has a radius cos θ times the Earth's radius, so each degree of longitude along it is 111.2 cos θ km. Here the angular distance is the difference in longitude.

questions.stem: Two places on the parallel 30°S have longitudes 120°E and 150°E. The distance between them along the parallel is closest to:
questions.explanation: The angular distance is 150° − 120° = 30°, so D = 111.2 × cos 30° × 30 ≈ 2889 km. Leaving out cos 30° gives 3336 km, which would be the distance only along the equator.

questions.stem: Two places on the equator are 120° of longitude apart. The distance between them along the equator is:
questions.explanation: On the equator θ = 0° and cos 0° = 1, so D = 111.2 × 120 = 13 344 km. The equator is a great circle, so this matches the meridian formula.

questions.stem: Two places on the parallel 40°N have longitudes 10°W and 25°E. The distance between them along the parallel is closest to:
questions.explanation: They are on opposite sides of the prime meridian, so the angular distance is 10° + 25° = 35°, and D = 111.2 × cos 40° × 35 ≈ 2981 km. Subtracting the longitudes gives 15° and about 1278 km.

questions.stem: Two places on the parallel 20°S are at 150°E and 160°W. The shorter distance between them along the parallel is closest to:
questions.explanation: Going across the 180° meridian, the angular distance is 360° − (150° + 160°) = 50°, so D = 111.2 × cos 20° × 50 ≈ 5225 km. Using 310° goes the long way round the parallel.

questions.stem: Two pairs of places each differ by 10° of longitude. The pair on the equator is about 1112 km apart. The pair on the parallel 60°S is about:
questions.explanation: Along the parallel 60°S, D = 111.2 × cos 60° × 10 = 111.2 × 0.5 × 10 = 556 km. Parallels shrink towards the poles, so the same difference in longitude covers a shorter distance than on the equator.

questions.stem: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is:
options: the local time in each Australian capital city during its daylight saving period
the time in a place exactly 180° of longitude from the prime meridian at Greenwich
the average of the local times of all the time zones across the world on that date
the international time standard, kept by atomic clocks, from which time zones are set
questions.explanation: UTC is the world's time standard, maintained by atomic clocks, and time zones are given as offsets such as UTC+10. For everyday purposes it is the same as Greenwich Mean Time.

questions.stem: Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) is:
options: the mean solar time on the prime meridian at Greenwich, London
the local time on the International Date Line in the Pacific
the time standard used only by ships and aircraft at sea level
the time on the equator at the point where it meets 180°
questions.explanation: GMT is the mean solar time at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, on the prime meridian (0°). It was the original basis for world time zones and is effectively the same as UTC for these calculations.

questions.stem: The International Date Line roughly follows:
questions.explanation: The International Date Line lies roughly along the 180° meridian in the Pacific Ocean, with bends to keep island groups on one date. Crossing it changes the calendar date.

questions.stem: A traveller crosses the International Date Line heading west, from Hawaii towards Australia. The calendar date:
questions.explanation: Places just west of the Date Line are a day ahead of places just east of it, so travelling west across it adds a day. Travelling east across it, from Australia towards the Americas, the date goes back one day.

questions.stem: The Earth turns through 360° in 24 hours. The number of degrees of longitude that corresponds to a time difference of 1 hour is:
questions.explanation: 360° ÷ 24 hours = 15° per hour. Equivalently, each degree of longitude corresponds to 4 minutes of time.

questions.stem: Ignoring time zone boundaries, two places whose longitudes differ by 45° have a time difference of:
questions.explanation: At 15° per hour, 45° ÷ 15 = 3 hours. Treating each degree as 1 minute gives 45 minutes, which forgets the 4 minutes per degree.

questions.stem: A time difference of 4 hours 20 minutes corresponds to a difference in longitude of:
questions.explanation: 4 hours 20 minutes = 4⅓ hours, and 4⅓ × 15 = 65°. Using 4.2 hours (reading 20 minutes as 0.2 h) gives 63°.

questions.stem: Ignoring time zone boundaries, the local time at 45°E is 3:00 pm. The local time at 15°W is:
questions.explanation: The longitude difference is 45° + 15° = 60°, which is 4 hours. Places to the west are behind, so the time at 15°W is 3:00 pm − 4 h = 11:00 am. Adding 4 hours gives 7:00 pm, the wrong direction.

questions.stem: Using longitude only, a place whose local time is 2 hours 40 minutes ahead of Greenwich lies at:
questions.explanation: 2 hours 40 minutes = 2⅔ hours, and 2⅔ × 15 = 40°. Places ahead of Greenwich are east of it, so the longitude is 40°E. 160 comes from converting the time to minutes and stopping there.

questions.stem: Queensland uses Australian Eastern Standard Time all year. Its time zone is:
questions.explanation: Queensland is 10 hours ahead of UTC and does not use daylight saving. UTC+11 is daylight saving time in New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania and the ACT.

questions.stem: In January, New South Wales uses daylight saving (UTC+11) and Queensland does not (UTC+10). When it is 9:00 am in Brisbane, the time in Sydney is:
questions.explanation: Daylight saving puts Sydney 1 hour ahead of Brisbane in summer, so 9:00 am in Brisbane is 10:00 am in Sydney. Outside daylight saving both use UTC+10, and the times are the same.

questions.stem: Western Australia uses UTC+8 all year. A Perth meeting starts at 9:00 am. The time in Brisbane (UTC+10) is:
questions.explanation: Brisbane is 10 − 8 = 2 hours ahead of Perth, so 9:00 am in Perth is 11:00 am in Brisbane. Subtracting the 2 hours gives 7:00 am, the wrong direction.

questions.stem: A Brisbane worker (UTC+10) phones a client in London when it is 3:00 pm in Brisbane. London is on UTC+0 at the time. The time in London is:
questions.explanation: London is 10 hours behind Brisbane, so 3:00 pm − 10 h = 5:00 am on the same day. Adding 10 hours instead gives 1:00 am the next day.

questions.stem: A football match in Perth (UTC+8) starts at 7:30 pm in December. Melbourne is on daylight saving (UTC+11). Brisbane is on UTC+10. When does it start in Brisbane and in Melbourne?
options: 9:30 pm in Brisbane and 9:30 pm in Melbourne
5:30 pm in Brisbane and 4:30 pm in Melbourne
10:30 pm in Brisbane and 9:30 pm in Melbourne
9:30 pm in Brisbane and 10:30 pm in Melbourne
questions.explanation: Brisbane is 2 hours ahead of Perth, giving 9:30 pm, and Melbourne on daylight saving is 3 hours ahead, giving 10:30 pm. Forgetting daylight saving would put Melbourne at the same time as Brisbane.

questions.stem: A flight leaves Brisbane (UTC+10) at 10:00 pm on Monday and takes 14 hours to reach Los Angeles, which is on UTC−8 at the time. The local arrival time in Los Angeles is:
questions.explanation: Departure is 12:00 noon Monday UTC, so arrival is 2:00 am Tuesday UTC, which is 2:00 am − 8 h = 6:00 pm Monday in Los Angeles. The flight crosses the Date Line heading east, so it lands at an earlier local time than it left.

questions.stem: In January, South Australia uses daylight saving (UTC+10.5) and Queensland does not (UTC+10). A webinar starts at 4:00 pm in Adelaide. The time in Brisbane is:
questions.explanation: Adelaide on daylight saving is half an hour ahead of Brisbane, so 4:00 pm in Adelaide is 3:30 pm in Brisbane. Adding the half hour gives 4:30 pm, the wrong direction.
